meta.subtitle: Off-price retailer with net cash: fiscal Q2 2027 sales up 5% with help from tariff refunds; a HOLD that sits close to BUY

analystCommentary: We rate The TJX Companies HOLD with a target range of $135 to $150, against a price of $131.59 on September 24, 2026. The second quarter of fiscal 2027, the thirteen weeks ended August 1, 2026, was strong on its face, with net sales {+ up 5% +} to $15.2 billion and a higher pre-tax margin. Part of that quarter will not repeat on its own: TJX recognized a $219 million net benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds and has booked no receivable for further refunds. The underlying model looks sound, with positive comp sales, a growing store base and more cash than debt. Our probability-weighted value lands just short of the BUY line, so the call is close, and the valuation section shows how small a change would move it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: The TJX Companies, Inc. is an off-price apparel and home fashions retailer, incorporated in 1962 and headquartered in Framingham, Massachusetts. It describes itself as the leading off-price apparel and home fashions retailer in the U.S. and worldwide, selling a rapidly changing assortment below full-price retailers' regular prices. According to the 10-Q, TJX operates over 5,200 stores through four segments: in the U.S., Marmaxx (TJ Maxx, Marshalls, tjmaxx.com and marshalls.com, with Sierra's results included) and HomeGoods (HomeGoods and Homesense); TJX Canada (Winners, HomeSense and Marshalls); and TJX International (TK Maxx, Homesense, tkmaxx.com, tkmaxx.de and tkmaxx.at in Europe, and TK Maxx in Australia). Its six e-commerce sites together amounted to approximately 2% of net sales in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. The data tables show a single consolidated segment, which disagrees with the 10-Q's four segments; we follow the 10-Q for the structure and quote no segment split, because the page carries none. In FY26, the fiscal year that ended in early 2026, revenue was $60.4 billion, net income $5.5 billion and diluted EPS $4.87.

thesis.body: TJX grows through comp-sales gains and new stores, and turns that growth into free cash flow that it largely returns to shareholders. The latest quarter added to that pattern: comps rose in both apparel and home, the store base grew, the long-term store target went up and the pre-tax margin widened. We do not treat the quarter's margin as the new run-rate, because a tariff-refund benefit that may not recur helped it, and the company does not say how much of the gain came from refunds rather than markon. At $131.59 the shares trade at 24.7x FY27E consensus EPS, a multiple that needs the growth to continue. Our scenarios give modest upside if it does and a real downside if it stalls, which nets to a HOLD that sits close to BUY.

catalysts: Further IEEPA refunds: TJX estimates it paid approximately $490 million of IEEPA-related tariffs and has received $331 million so far; any further refund is unrecorded and would add to results (see Risks for the limits).
Store growth: TJX raised its long-term global store target to 7,500, and its store base is still growing (see Growth).
Comp momentum: comps rose in the latest quarter and the six months, driven by both basket and transactions (see Growth).
Street support: most covering analysts rate the shares Buy, and every Street target sits above today's price (see Valuation).
risks: Refund non-recurrence: the refund benefit that helped the latest quarter's margin may not repeat, and further refunds are uncertain.
Unexplained price weakness: the shares trade near their 52-week low for reasons no source on the page gives; we weight the Bear partly on it (see Valuation).
Store labor costs: higher store wage and payroll costs helped lift the SG&A ratio in the latest quarter.
Competition and channel: some competitors are larger, and the business is primarily in stores while consumer e-commerce spending may keep rising (see Business and Moat).
Merchant execution: misjudged buying can leave excess inventory and force markdowns.

financials.incomeCommentary:
In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, the thirteen weeks ended August 1, 2026, net sales were $15.2 billion, {+ up 5% +} year over year from $14.4 billion. The company attributes the increase to a 4% rise in comp sales and growth in non-comp sales, partly offset by a 1% negative impact from currency. Diluted EPS was {+ $1.36 +} against $1.10, and the pre-tax profit margin rose {+ 1.9 percentage points +} to 13.3% from 11.4%. Two cost lines moved in opposite directions. The cost-of-sales ratio, including buying and occupancy costs, fell to 66.6% from 69.3%, which the company attributes to a net benefit from tariff refunds and favorable merchandise margin due to higher markon. The SG&A ratio {- rose 0.8 percentage points -} to 20.3% from 19.5%, which it attributes to incremental compensation accruals tied to the refunds and incremental store wage and payroll costs. The refund arithmetic is the company's: $331 million of IEEPA refunds recognized in cost of sales, less $112 million of incremental incentive compensation and bonus accruals, for a net benefit of $219 million. The MD&A does not split the cost-of-sales improvement between refunds and markon, so the page cannot show how much of the margin gain will last. For the six months ended August 1, 2026, net sales rose 7% to $29.5 billion and the pre-tax margin was 12.7% against 10.9%.

Over the five fiscal years shown, revenue grew from $48.6 billion in FY22 to $60.4 billion in FY26, with annual growth between +2.9% and +8.6%. Gross margin dipped to 27.6% in FY23 and then widened each year to 31.0% in FY26; the trailing-twelve-month gross margin of 32.0% includes the refund quarter. Net income rose from $3.3 billion to $5.5 billion and diluted EPS from $2.70 to $4.87. The vendor tables carry no operating-income or EBITDA line, so we read profitability through the pre-tax margin the company reports.
financials.balanceCommentary: TJX holds more cash than debt. At the end of FY26, cash and short-term investments were $6.2 billion against total debt of $2.9 billion, for net debt of -$3.4 billion. Net debt has stayed negative in all five years shown, moving between -$2.1 billion in FY23 and the FY26 level. Total equity rose each year, from $6.0 billion in FY22 to $10.2 billion in FY26. The current ratio has eased from 1.27 in FY22 to 1.14 in FY26 and 1.15 on a trailing basis; with net cash behind it, we read that as working-capital management rather than strain. Consolidated average per-store inventories, which include distribution centers but exclude goods in transit and the e-commerce sites, were up 2% at the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2027, below the quarter's sales growth.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow rose from $3.1 billion in FY22 to $6.9 billion in FY26, while capital expenditure rose from $1.0 billion to $2.0 billion. Free cash flow reached $4.9 billion in FY26, an 8.1% FCF margin, after $4.2 billion in FY25. Share repurchases were $2.5 billion in each of FY24, FY25 and FY26, and dividends paid rose from $1.3 billion in FY22 to $1.8 billion in FY26. The proxy puts FY26 shareholder returns at $4.3 billion, which FY26 free cash flow covered, so the payout did not need new borrowing.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $131.59, TJX trades at 24.4x trailing earnings, 2.3x sales and 17.4x trailing EV/EBITDA on the vendor's figures; the statement tables carry no EBITDA line, so the EV/EBITDA cannot be checked against them. The forward P/E labelled next-twelve-month is 24.7x, which matches the price over FY27E consensus EPS of $5.33, so we treat it as the current-year multiple and use it as the like-for-like reference. On FY28E consensus EPS of $5.79 the multiple is about 22.7x. The trailing P/E sits just below the current-year multiple, which suggests the vendor's trailing earnings already run slightly ahead of FY27E consensus; we do not lean on this, because the page shows neither the trailing window nor whether consensus includes the refund quarter. The trailing FCF yield is 4.1% and the dividend yields 1.47%. The page carries no peer multiples and no history of TJX's own multiple, so we do not call the shares cheap or expensive against either. The Street is more positive than we are: 18 of 22 analysts rate the stock Buy and none Sell, and targets run from $136.00 to $198.00, with a consensus of $169.80 (+29.0%) and a median of $175.00. The shares sit near the low end of a $122.78 to $170.00 52-week range.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Comps stay positive, store growth continues toward the 7,500 target, markon holds and further IEEPA refunds arrive. The shares recover to their 52-week high of $170.00, close to the Street consensus target of $169.80. We anchor to the 52-week high because the market paid that price within the past year.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Comps and store growth continue near the latest pace, the refund benefit does not recur and higher markon roughly offsets store wage costs, so FY28E consensus EPS of $5.79 is met. We value it at 24.7x, today's current-year multiple held a year out, for $143.01.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Comps slow, the markon gain reverses, store wage costs keep rising and no further refunds arrive, so earnings fall back to FY26's diluted EPS of $4.87. We assume 22x, below today's current-year multiple because growth has reversed, but not far below the 22.7x the market pays on FY28E because the store base and the net-cash balance sheet are intact, for $107.14.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Each scenario values the shares a year out. The Base holds today's current-year multiple and rolls it onto FY28E EPS, so it is today's anchor plus one year of consensus growth, and that anchor decides the label. The case for a higher multiple is the runway in the raised store target, funded from a net-cash balance sheet. The case for a lower one is that FY27E consensus may already include the one-time refund benefit, which would flatter the growth the multiple pays for. We see these as roughly balanced and hold the multiple; each turn of multiple moves the Base by the amount of FY28E EPS.

The weights rest on different evidence. Bull gets 25% because the operating record leans its way, with comps up in every period on the page and, per the proxy, in every division in FY26, and because most of the Street rates the shares Buy; it stays well below Base because the refund upside is uncertain, since the company says further refunds may not equal what it paid and it has recorded no receivable. Bear gets 20% because the shares have fallen toward their 52-week low, which no source on the page explains, and because the MD&A calls the tariff and demand outlook uncertain; it stays below Bull because nothing on the page yet shows comps slowing. Base gets the remaining 55%.

The weighted fair value is $142.58, an expected upside of +8.4% against a bear-case downside of -18.6%, for a reward/risk of 0.45×. That derives HOLD, short of the +10.0% BUY line. The call is close on the upside: moving five points of weight from Bear to Bull, or a Base multiple less than one turn higher, derives BUY. Moving five points from Bull to Bear, or holding the Base at the multiple the market pays today on FY28E, which puts it at about today's price, keeps HOLD, and SELL would need a much larger change. Our $135 to $150 range brackets the Base and the weighted value.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The data tables carry one consolidated segment, and the excerpt gives no segment sales or profit, so we assess the business as a whole; the four operating segments are described in the overview. The one segment-level fact on the page is the store plan: the raised long-term target adds 300 stores to Marmaxx's goal and 200 to HomeGoods'. TJX Canada and TJX International report in local currencies that are translated into dollars, which we treat under Risks.

moatFactors.name: Value gap
moatFactors.body: TJX sells at prices generally 20% to 60% below full-price retailers' regular prices on comparable merchandise, every day. The 10-K sets the condition: if merchandise is not bought at prices sufficiently below what conventional retailers pay, the value gap may not hold in some segments, banners, categories or geographies.

moatFactors.name: Opportunistic buying
moatFactors.body: Merchants buy throughout the year, much of it for the current or immediately upcoming season, and the 10-K calls opportunistic buying a key element of the strategy. The company says it believes it can continue to mitigate tariff pressures through its sourcing model, and the latest quarter's markon gain (see Financials) is consistent with that.

moatFactors.name: Lean, flexible inventory
moatFactors.body: Lean inventory and frequent turns let TJX expand and contract categories as tastes change, per the 10-K. Per-store inventories growing more slowly than sales in the latest quarter (see Financials) fits that discipline.

moatFactors.name: Banner and market breadth
moatFactors.body: The store base spans the U.S., Canada, Europe and Australia under several banners. Per the April 2026 proxy, each division delivered comp growth of 4% or better in FY26, so growth did not rest on one banner.

businessMoat.durability: The page supports a durable model: revenue rose in every year shown and gross margin widened in each of the last three. The page covers only five years, so the long track record the proxy describes rests on the company's own account. The 10-K, filed in March 2026, names the threats. Some competitors are larger and hold greater financial resources, new competitors frequently enter, and TJX could be at a disadvantage if competitors use technologies including artificial intelligence more effectively. Consumer e-commerce spending may continue to increase while TJX's business is primarily in brick-and-mortar stores. We rate the moat wide because the value gap and the buying model have held through the tariff pressure on the page, but merchants have to re-earn it each season.

points: Comp growth in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and in the six months, when comps rose 5%, came from a higher average basket and more customer transactions, with home comps ahead of apparel in both periods.
Store count and selling square footage each rose about 3% year over year to August 1, 2026, and TJX raised its long-term global store target to 7,500 stores.
Consensus expects FY27E revenue of about $64 billion (+6%) and FY28E revenue of $68 billion.
E-commerce stays small, at about 2% of net sales across six sites in each of the last two second quarters, so it adds little to growth on the page.

management.leadership: The April 2026 proxy names the Named Executive Officers for FY26: Ernie Herrman, Chief Executive Officer and President; John Klinger, Senior Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer; Carol Meyrowitz, Executive Chairman; and Douglas Mizzi and Kenneth Canestrari, each Senior Executive Vice President, Group President. The proxy says each has decades of experience with the off-price business and that the company remains highly focused on management continuity and succession planning. That experience suits a model that relies on merchant judgment. The excerpt gives no detail on the succession plan itself, so we cannot assess it.
management.capitalAllocation: TJX funds both store growth and shareholder returns from its own cash flow, and FY26 returns fit within free cash flow (see Financials). The 10-Q reports a further $1.3 billion returned through repurchases and dividends in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. Debt has not been needed to fund the payout (see the balance sheet). On our scenarios the shares trade a little below fair value, so repurchases at today's price add modest value per share if the Base holds and destroy some if the Bear plays out.
management.governance: The DEF 14A filed April 30, 2026 gives the Corporate Governance Committee responsibility for reviewing and approving related-person transactions. It lists relatives employed by TJX who received compensation for FY26 and the beginning of FY27: two adult children of Peter Benjamin ($228,282 and $148,979), an adult child and the spouse of an adult child of Kenneth Canestrari ($238,763 and $305,821), and an adult child of Ms. Meyrowitz ($424,320). The proxy says their pay was consistent with other Associates at their levels and responsibilities. We see these as small for a company of TJX's size and not a governance concern on their own. In 2025, 94% of votes cast supported the say-on-pay proposal, and incentive results for FY26 and FY24-26 were based 100% on objective financial goals. The excerpt does not cover board composition, director independence or insider ownership, so we do not assess them.

idiosyncratic: Refund realization: TJX has recorded no receivable for further IEEPA refunds, and it says any further refunds may not equal the full amount of tariffs paid and remain subject to legal, regulatory or administrative developments. If none arrive, the second quarter of fiscal 2028 will be compared with a quarter that held the refund benefit.

Merchant execution: the 10-K says the opportunistic model places considerable discretion with merchants. If they misjudge demand, TJX may carry excess inventory and need markdowns, or run short of goods.

Store labor costs: the Base assumes higher markon offsets the store wage and payroll costs that lifted the SG&A ratio (see Financials). If it does not, the margin gives back part of its gain and the Bear becomes more likely.

Currency: TJX Canada and TJX International are translated into dollars, and the company says significant rate changes can cause meaningful variations in net sales and earnings per share. Mark-to-market on inventory hedges also moves cost of sales between periods.
risks.systemic: Tariffs are the main macro risk on the page. TJX says tariffs have led to significant volatility in the global economy, and that their effect on its direct and indirect imports, vendor and competitor pricing, consumer demand, tariff pass-throughs and retaliatory tariffs remains uncertain. In February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs, and U.S. Customs and Border Patrol is handling refund claims through a phased process. The 10-K adds that inflationary pressures and global supply chain disruptions have affected inventory execution in the past. Consumer demand is the channel through which these would reach TJX: its comps depend on transactions and basket size, and a weaker consumer would slow both.

body: We rate TJX HOLD with a target range of $135 to $150 against $131.59. The weighted fair value of $142.58 gives an expected upside of +8.4% against a bear-case downside of -18.6% (reward/risk 0.45×), just short of the BUY line. The business case is sound; the price already pays for it, and the scenarios above, not the quality of the quarter, set the call.

On unchanged scenarios the label moves with the price. A decline of a few dollars, still above the 52-week low of $122.78, would derive BUY, and a price just above the top of our range would derive SELL. On the fundamentals, we would raise the Base if the second half of fiscal 2027 shows the pre-tax margin holding without new refunds, and lower it if comps slow or the SG&A ratio keeps rising.
